title: Cell Size and the Surface Area-to-Volume Ratio
subject: AP Biology

chunks.text: Materials such as oxygen, glucose, and ions enter a cell through its surface (the plasma membrane), and wastes such as carbon dioxide leave through that surface. The cell's volume determines how much resource it consumes and how much waste it produces.
The surface-area-to-volume ratio describes the relationship between a cell's surface area, which delivers materials, and its volume, which demands them. A high ratio means efficient exchange.
For a cube with side length s, surface area equals 6 times s squared and volume equals s cubed. The surface-area-to-volume ratio is found by dividing surface area by volume.
For a cube with 1 micrometer sides, surface area is 6 square micrometers, volume is 1 cubic micrometer, and the surface-area-to-volume ratio is 6 to 1.
For a cube with 10 micrometer sides, surface area is 600 square micrometers, volume is 1000 cubic micrometers, and the surface-area-to-volume ratio is 0.6 to 1.

When a cell grows, surface area increases with the square of its size while volume increases with the cube of its size. Because volume grows faster than surface area, the surface-area-to-volume ratio decreases as a cell gets larger.
Doubling the side length of a cube increases surface area fourfold but increases volume eightfold, cutting the surface-area-to-volume ratio in half. Surface area and volume do not scale together.

The rate at which materials cross a membrane depends on surface area, while the rate at which a cell consumes resources and produces waste depends on volume. If volume outpaces surface area, the membrane cannot import nutrients or export wastes fast enough.

Diffusion is fast over short distances but slow over long distances, with the time required increasing roughly with the square of the distance. In a small cell molecules diffuse quickly, but in a large cell the trip from membrane to center would be too slow to sustain metabolism.
Most cells remain small because staying small keeps the surface-area-to-volume ratio high enough for efficient exchange of materials.

Eukaryotic cells contain many internal membranes and organelles, which create extra surface area for reactions and transport without increasing the cell's overall size. This is one benefit of compartmentalization.
For a fixed volume, a flat or elongated cell has a higher surface-area-to-volume ratio than a compact sphere. This is why red blood cells are flattened discs and nerve cells are long and thin.
Microvilli are microscopic projections on the cells lining the small intestine that greatly increase the surface area available for absorbing nutrients.
Alveoli are tiny air sacs in the lungs that create an enormous surface area for gas exchange, allowing oxygen to enter and carbon dioxide to leave the blood efficiently.
Root hairs are thin extensions of plant root cells that increase the surface area for absorbing water and minerals from the soil.

Cristae are folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane that increase surface area for the electron transport chain. Thylakoids stacked into grana increase surface area inside chloroplasts. Both are organelle-level surface-area maximizers.

To calculate and compare surface-area-to-volume ratios, find surface area and volume using the correct shape formulas, divide surface area by volume, and conclude that the cell or shape with the higher ratio exchanges materials more efficiently relative to its needs.

Surface-area-to-volume relationships also affect whole animals: heat is generated by body volume but lost through body surface. Small animals have a high ratio and lose heat quickly, while large animals have a low ratio and retain heat easily.
An elephant has large thin ears that add surface area to help dissipate excess body heat, an example of an organism increasing surface area to solve an exchange problem.
There are no cell-sized large animals and no animal-sized cells because the surface-area-to-volume constraint sets physical limits on how large a single cell can be.

On AP Biology free-response and data questions about surface area to volume, full credit requires both calculating the ratios (showing surface area and volume) and interpreting them, such as concluding that a smaller cell with a higher ratio exchanges materials more efficiently.
When given a graph of surface-area-to-volume ratio versus cell size, the correct interpretation is that the ratio decreases as size increases, which limits how large a functioning cell can be.
